text.title: Verification Rung Placement Rules
text.summary: Six rules for routing a check to the cheapest instrument that can detect its defect. R1 places; R2 is the discipline that keeps the placement honest; R3-R6 govern what each rung is allowed to do once a check lands there.

rule.statement: For every check, ask three questions in order and stop at the first yes. Q1 — can this be decided by reading the artefact's bytes, with no model, no network and no reference to what a reasonable person would have wanted? Then RUNG 1: write it as code. Q2 — does it need the real system to run, but the correct answer is mechanically comparable (an ID, a set, a rank, a boolean, a count)? Then RUNG 2: write a labelled case; the label is the asset, the harness is replaceable. Q3 — does it need a judgement about quality with no mechanical ground truth? Then RUNG 3, and only if you would personally re-read that scenario before every release anyway. Anything left is RUNG H: read it yourself. The record MUST state, per check, which question first answered yes.
rule.rationale: 528 broken `methodology_refs`/`playbook_refs` across 5,744 published MDX files — 18,107 refs checked, 69 distinct phantom slugs, down from 883 after a manifest fix. The class had been caught by a review agent, i.e. paid for at rung-3 prices, and a ~20-line rung-1 validator catches all of it for zero tokens on every commit. The defect was never hard; the instrument was wrong.

rule.statement: A check may live on a rung only if it CANNOT live on the rung below, and the record MUST carry the one-line reason for every check placed above rung 1. "A model would be easier to write" is not a reason — a model is never easier to maintain. Rung inflation (reaching for the fanciest available instrument) and rung deflation (writing an elaborate deterministic check for something that genuinely requires judgement) are both violations of this rule; the first is more common and more expensive.
rule.rationale: A check on rung 2 that a regex could do runs perhaps nightly instead of on every commit — three orders of magnitude less often — and costs money each time. A check on rung 3 that an `==` could do is a coin flip you are paying for: the best debiased judge configuration tested reaches only κ=0.549 (arXiv:2604.23178, TMLR 2026), so the expensive instrument is also the less reliable one for anything mechanically decidable.

rule.statement: At rung 1, a check that decides by exact rule MAY block; a check that decides by heuristic MUST only flag. The record MUST mark each rung-1 check `exact: true|false`, and any check with `exact: false` MUST have `action: flag`. Density measures, style detectors and anything tuned by threshold are heuristics regardless of how deterministic their code is.
rule.rationale: The reference implementation splits HARD findings (block, some auto-fixable) from FLAG findings (report, never block — documented as "heuristics with false-positive risk"). Determinism is not the same property as correctness: a blocking check with false positives trains the operator to bypass the gate, which costs more than the check ever saved.

rule.statement: Rung-3 checks MUST be pairwise (champion vs challenger, order-swapped, disagreements recorded as UNDECIDED and not counted) and MUST report a win/loss/undecided distribution, never a mean or an absolute score. The total rung-3 scenario count MUST be declared as a budget and MUST NOT exceed 15. Formatting MUST be normalised across both candidates before judging.
rule.rationale: The best debiased configuration tested reaches 71.0% human agreement, κ=0.549 — "moderate" on Landis-Koch, below any sane gating threshold, so a judge is triage rather than a gate. Style bias measures 0.10-0.76 (judges prefer markdown) while position bias is only ≤0.04, so normalising formatting matters roughly 19x more than swapping order. Claude judges prefer concise output (−0.12): a bias aligned with your own house style is the dangerous kind. Beyond ~15 scenarios you no longer have a rung-3 suite, you have a slow rung-2 suite with a random number generator in it.

rule.statement: A person reading the output is a legitimate verification instrument with the highest judgement ceiling available and the only one that can notice a problem nobody thought to check for. It MUST be recorded as `rung: H` and described as a manual review gate — never as "deterministic", because the operational property of that word is repeatability without you. State its cost in founder-hours in the same breath as its value. Every time rung H catches something, the record MUST log what was found and which rung the resulting check was pushed down to; a rung-H entry that has never produced a pushed-down check is a defect being re-discovered every session.
rule.rationale: Manual review is reliable, not repeatable, not scalable, not automatable, and not a regression test — it can tell you whether the thing in front of you is acceptable, never that something changed. Every automated rung exists to buy human attention back, not to replace human judgement. Human review is where new checks are discovered; it should not be where the same check is repeated.

rule.statement: Cadence is a function of rung, not of preference. Rung 1 runs in the pre-commit hook and every CI run — it is the only rung whose cost does not scale with how often it runs. Rung 2 runs nightly and on every change to a prompt, the corpus, or a model pin. Rung 3 runs before a release and on a champion/challenger decision, deliberately, with the token bill in view. Rung H runs on anything new and on anything rungs 1-3 flagged as ambiguous. Rungs 2 and 3 MUST NOT be wired into a pre-commit hook.
rule.rationale: A hook that costs money and minutes per commit gets disabled within a week, and then you have nothing rather than something. A rung-1 sweep across ~2,600 methodology directories completes in seconds to low minutes and is entirely I/O-bound, so its marginal cost per extra check is near zero.
